With the sequel coming very soon, I decided it was finally time to go back to this after only playing a couple chapters when it first came out. This game truly is the best non-strategy Warhammer experience from both a gameplay and lore/story perspective. What a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ diamond in the rough. I only hope that SM2 will continue this trend!

It is a tad strange that the final boss is relegated to QTE's but I will chock that up to 2011 games being 2011 games.

In the grim darkness of the far future, some badass third person shootery occurs - 8.5/10

Captain Titus is one of many Captains in the Ultramarines chapter. While his brothers are among the most conventional of the adept, highly skilled and devotedly motivated metahumans with extensive augmentations, Titus is one of the unique individuals that have not become completely devoted to dogma. The Imperium of Man itself is dogma above all else. Those who dare defy this norm risk temptation from the Forces of Chaos or may even find themselves collaborating with the Xenos, who wish nothing but dismay and genocide upon humanity. Yet, there is the Inquisition, which sanctions the breaking of dogmatic practice and ritualistic legalism if it means defending humanity. Who knew, that on this damned world, Titus' greatest enemy may just be within the Imperium itself?

There is really no reason to not spoil the game, as its overly a decade and then some, as well as being one of the most well known games within the 40k IP. Titus is a unique individual, able to resist the Warp or at least, circumvent the results of having come into direct contact with it. It reminds me a lot of the Firewarrior game's novelization, whereas the protagonist is far from being a heretic, yet finds himself enabled by some Chaos-aligned power beyond him. The dissonance of this unique situation allows for a surprisingly nuanced story, even though the plot itself is nothing spectacular otherwise.

The characters are about what one expects, with the villains being among the most enjoyable and well written. Despite this, Titus himself is dull only at first and the more familiar you are with 40k lore, the more of an anomaly he ends up being. Despite being betrayed to the Inquisition for some very sound reasons, his motivations are completely understandable and he is entirely sound in not trusting the Inquisition to the 'Chekov's Gun' of the plot. But on this more recent play through, in preparation for the upcoming Space Marine 2, I encountered something interesting I had no previously noticed.

The plot itself raises a theological question, that fits masterfully in the 40k setting. Titus is not so much a reformer of any sort, in fact, he is more like a liberal getting arrested by the Soviet NKVD for questioning some draconian law or adherence to a certain doctrine's dogmatic canon. He is hardly a Martin Luther or a Jan Hus, but he definitely fights against the conventional mold of his organization and the Imperium as a whole.

He does not critique the Codex, nor does he wish it to be abandoned or see himself above it. Instead, Titus is not a legalist. He does not believe that the Codex itself will exclusively lead to the absolute good, he, himself, at the end states it is actually the integrity of the Space Marine as an individual, that will validate the Codex. To outsiders, and especially to a young acolyte of the Ultramarines who only sees the absolutism of the Codex, this plain and outright heresy. Ironically, the Pavel Morozov-esque betrayer (I'd say Judas but the gain was not monetary for him, merely ideological and spiritual) ignores that the Inquisition is the complete embodiment of this compromise. Their activities are outright heretical (this is pivotal to the plot itself in the individual Inquisitor Drogan) yet are sanctioned by the merit of their mission and individual integrity, enforced by the necessity of, once again, the mission.

Titus fulfilled his mission to the end and in Messianic sacrifice, he submits to the Inquisition and the unfair circumstance forced upon him. Incredible. While the story is not so strongly told, it is hard to ignore how strongly this actually fits into the IP so well and remains impactful. Which truly elevates it as one of the stronger 40k games narratives, despite presenting not as much as others due to budgetary restraints. 

Titus, also, may be named after the Emperor who, as a general, would later cause the mass exodus of Roman Jews from Judea. He, himself, was a lover of the Jewish Queen at the time. Interestingly, this same Titus of history, (the II, I believe) went on to say "there is no glory in defeating a people forsaken by their own god". I find this very interesting. Titus of Space Marine, is in a way, a Jesus-like figure who offers a new understanding of the Word aka the Codex Astartes, in this case, then goes onto fulfill prophecy literally and directly, only to be hated by the legalists (the Pharisees of biblical lore, but in this context, the Inqusition of the Imperium of Man) and subject to cruel punishment. 

Titus undergoes no transfiguration, yet. Space Marine is the first parts of the Gospel of the New Covenant, where as Space Marine 2 will be the post-gospel New Testament of Titus lore, I am sure of it. We have yet to see Titus' transfiguration, as we have not even seen his crucifixion yet, but his Judas scene at the end truly makes the game worth it.

All that being said, I love Space Marine. Its not exactly the most fun game, I surely wouldn't recommend paying the current price for it (get a key or wait for sale) and its honestly only worth a few playthroughs spread out over long periods of time, but it is special. It is the Batman Begins of 40k games, showing us a new light and potential and I am hoping Space Marine 2 will be the series' Dark Knight.

My only complaints is that the gameplay, even for 2011, is a tad dated. But this can be rectified, in terms of boredom of repetitive combat, by taking frequent breaks. Just because you can beat this game in a single sitting, doesn't mean you should. 

The music is a bit lackluster, although there is one track that is absolutely fantastic and its existence is far too short lived, but that almost makes it more effective. Fighting the Orkz can be really repetitive, but by the time you face Chaos, the game gets tremendously better for its triumphant final third. But I did get really tired of the chainsword's steely, industrial growl and the WAAAAAGH of certain Orkz Nobz. Ironically, I have a similar complaint about the old Firewarrior game on PS2 and PC. The chainsword in that game was also repetitive and repeated far too often to a grating effect. Not only that, but instead of constantly hearing the same WAAAAGH over and over, you heard Imperial Guardsmen constantly uttering "IT'S QUIET" to themselves, ironically, at ear-watering decibels. 

I remember playing this game for the first time on console when it first came out. In fact, I think it was one of the first games I ever pre-ordered (ironically, for the multiplayer) besides Dead Space 2. I actually played the multiplayer of both this game and Dead Space 2's with that very same person. Thus, this game is very nostalgic for me. I also played it with my cousins a few time and for them, I think it was their formal introduction into the 40k IP.

40k itself, as an IP and as a setting, is flawed, but when you allow yourself to enjoy it simply for what it is - there are few settings as pleasurable.

I owe a lot to the 40k fandom. I've encountered so many people in fundamental parts of my youth and young adulthood through 40k. A girlfriend, a sworn enemy and rival, friends I have talked to for over a decade and a half. I've also known some very prominent online artists and writers, in the industry and in new social media fandoms to this day, who first cut their teeth on the Warhammer 40k universe. 

The game, itself, is honestly 7/10 mid. But being a GOOD 40k game, to a 40k fan, it might as well be a near perfect 9.5/10. Even for a casual fan or a less than enthused gamer picking this up, it has charming 10/10 moments that really make the full experience worth it. There are a few difficulty spikes that really grinded my balls here and there, but nothing that some patience and a break couldn't help resolve. The game does have jank, but all 40k games do. The hitboxes here and getting stuck on the environment, time to time, would have been much more frustrating if I hadn't dealt with worse in the original Dawn of War 1.
Amazing Story and Badass game play. Enjoyed every moment of the game and all of the action.
